\section*{Discussion}

\subsection*{What the test shows and what it does not}

The test asked a question with a yes or no answer, and the answer was no. In the deciding run a crawl ordered by the coupled walk reached the contracts with the most user-account demand sooner than a breadth-first crawl, but a crawl ordered by a plain count, the number of contracts already visited that pay or authorize the candidate, reached them sooner than the walk on both importances. The sensitivities left that reading in place, and at the other freeze the same mode gave the same signs. On the contract graph of this rollup, with in-edges visible, coupling allowance and transfer edges in one walk did not order a crawl better than counting backlinks.

The test does not show that walks are useless for discovery. One walk beat the count it smooths: the crawl ordered by AWP, a transfer walk with value and time weights and restarts at contracts that sent recently, had the highest area in the deciding run and lay above the transfer backlink count on both importances in all four runs. The coupled walk lay below AWP, and its own transfer layer walked alone lay below the transfer backlink count, so walking the transfer layer was not enough by itself. The two transfer walks differ in their weights and in their restarts, and the test does not separate the two. The result also depends on what a visit reveals. Where a visit shows out-edges only, as on the web, the coupled walk led both comparators at both freezes, under a mode that the protocol's rule made a sensitivity analysis. In that mode the frontier holds only contracts that visited contracts point to, the counts tie on nearly every pick, and the coupled walk and the transfer walks rarely tie; we did not test whether this is the reason. Even there, the comparison nearest to the web experiment did not come out as on the web: on the hot set of contracts with the most backlinks, the backlink ordering was sooner than the coupled walk in all four runs. The contract graph differs from a university's web in ways that may matter, among them a hub that ends 441,612 transfer pairs, seeds drawn by hash and not a home page, and weighted layers; the test does not say which of these accounts for the difference.

Two readings of the same crawls should be held together. Counted over the hot sets, every ordering was far from the ideal order and not far from a random one: after a tenth of the visits no crawl in the comparison had reached more than a quarter of either hot set. Weighted by dollars, the coupled walk had visited contracts that hold most of the inflow and most of the authorized value of the universe within the first hundredth of the visits, sooner than the backlink ordering, which caught up within the first tenth; AWP reached most of the inflow as early but less than half of the authorized value. The demand of user accounts is concentrated in a few contracts that the walks find within the first visits, and the long remainder of the hot sets is what the statistic of the test measures. The value-weighted reading is reported by the protocol as curves only and has no interval.

The allowance layer between contracts is thin, and the test says little in its favor. Under the balance cap most allowances between contracts count for nothing, because the authorizing contract holds no balance of the token at the freeze. Only 16,776 capped allowance pairs lie in the universe of the deciding run against 2,383,503 transfer pairs, the walks on the allowance layer alone were not above the allowance backlink count on inflow, and adding the layer to the transfer layer raised the area by 0.0024 and 0.0137. By value the layer did more: after a tenth of the visits the orderings that read both layers had visited contracts holding 85.9\% to 87.0\% of the user-authorized value, the orderings that read allowances only 68.4\% to 86.5\%, and the orderings that read transfers only about half of it (S1 Table). Contracts authorize one another much less than users authorize contracts, and a graph of contracts sees only the first kind.

\subsection*{The walks against their counts out of window}

Out of window the two edge types measure different things: scores built on allowances rank which spenders later gain new approvals, and scores built on transfers which later gain new senders. Propagating along the allowance edge added nothing. EndorseRank fell below the count of approving contracts in both windows, with either restart rule, and the closed form says why this is unsurprising for most spenders: there the walk is the count, with each approval scaled by its recency and divided by its owner's total approval weight. On the transfer side AWP was slightly above its count on the whole cohorts and, in W0, below it among the spenders that a contract had already paid, so its small lead comes from the spenders that the count leaves at zero. That a count is hard to beat fits preferential attachment and link-prediction practice~\cite{barabasi1999scaling,libennowell2007link}. All of these coefficients are small, the labels count mostly user accounts that the graph does not hold, and about 27\% of each cohort scores zero, so the comparisons say more about the order of the scores than about how well any of them predicts.

\subsection*{Practical implications}

The results support modest advice for those who must choose which contracts to look at first. A wallet, an explorer or an auditor that reads the chain's logs sees both who paid a contract and whom it paid. In that setting the number of distinct contracts that pay or authorize a contract ordered a crawl at least as well as the coupled walk, at no solver cost, and a transfer walk with AWP's weights and restarts did somewhat better at the price of a solve at every recompute. An integrator that follows only whom a contract itself pays and authorizes is closer to the other mode, where the coupled walk and the transfer walks led; that result carries no verdict here and should be tested before it is relied on. For ranking which spender contracts will gain new approvers, the count of approving contracts ranked above EndorseRank in both windows. For new senders AWP and the transfer in-degree were close, with the count ahead, in the first window, among contracts that were already paid by others.

None of these orderings finds the contracts that users rely on efficiently. The best crawl was far from the ideal order, and most of the first tenth of the visits of every ordering went to contracts with no user-account demand. The contracts that hold most of the demand by value are few, and the walks on the transfer layer reach most of the inflow within the first hundredth of the visits; the difficulty is the long tail. A count of contract backlinks tells how widely other contracts use a contract, not what the contract will do with an allowance: a phishing contract can be paid and authorized by contracts that its operator deploys, at the cost of a deployment and a balance each, and a new contract scores low whatever its code. A low count is a reason to look closer, and a high count is no reason to sign. None of these scores is a security audit, and whether a score of this kind could later serve as one input to credit decisions about contracts was not tested.

\subsection*{Limitations}

The evidence comes from one chain, two freezes that share nine months of their score windows, and five tokens, so other rollups and Layer-1 networks would need new data~\cite{werner2022sok}, contracts that are used only through other tokens are outside the graph, and native ether enters only as WETH. The contract-graph analysis and the discovery-order test were defined after the registered results were known, so the tokens, price source, windows, account-type rules, balance cap, constants, importance measures and the test's statistic were all chosen by people who had seen those results; the test decides no rule of the plan or the registration, and its verdict is not a registered result. The result depends on the reveal mode, and the mode that decides was named by a rule on the structure of one freeze.

The allowance layer between contracts is thin. The pilot found a capped allowance in-edge on 0.54\% of the contracts of the SCC and OUT at $t_1$, below the protocol's threshold, and the test went on. At $\Tobs$ one owner contract holds 98,073 of the 115,006 capped allowance pairs, so the allowance-side results at $\Tobs$, namely the same-window checks, W1 and the closed form at $\Tobs$, lean on the approvals of a single contract, which the study does not identify; at $t_1$ the largest owner holds 256 pairs.

Account types are read from code at one block after the end of the data, and the smart-account rules find Safes and ERC-4337 accounts. Kinds they miss stay contracts: after the listed code families, 115,084 typed contracts still carry a \texttt{validateUserOp} selector and no paymaster selector without answering a canonical EntryPoint, and contracts that services create for each user, order or payment are not picked out. A contract that destroyed itself before the read counts as a user account. Addresses that sent no transaction and whose only counterparties are transaction senders are not typed and cannot be nodes; in an audit sample of 1,000 of them the reads found contract code other than a smart account's for 54, so some contracts that only user accounts use lie outside the graph. Balances are reconstructed from \texttt{Transfer} logs and matched \texttt{balanceOf} for 99.5\% of a sample, so tokens that change balances without such logs would be misread.

Coverage is partial: about a third of the matched cohort and 27\% of each spender cohort lie outside the union graph and score zero, which ties many members and lowers every coefficient. The labels count events around the cohort and mostly user accounts, which no score reads, and they are sparse counts of arrivals, which favor any score that tracks the current number of counterparties. The importance measures are sums of capped dollar amounts, the hot set of $I_A$ is every contract with a positive value, and the intervals of the test resample hot contracts with the 20 seeds fixed; under a bootstrap over the seeds two of the four decision intervals include zero. The schedule recomputes an ordering only after each growth of the visits by one fiftieth.

Every interval of the holdouts treats contracts as independent and the graphs as fixed, although spenders share owners, so the intervals are probably too narrow; the analyses use only 400 resamples, and no interval is adjusted for multiplicity. AWP's parameters are our choices, as its paper gives none. Approvals older than the score window are not read even when they are still in force, an \texttt{Approval} event can record the remainder after a spend as well as a grant, and allowances inside managers such as Permit2 are unseen. No outcome outside the chain was available as an importance label, and no causal claim is made.

%======================================================================
\section*{Conclusions}

Does PageRank find the smart contracts that users rely on sooner than counting? On the contract graph of Arbitrum One the answer depends on the walk and on what a crawl can see, and for the walk on which the test's decision rested it is no. In the run that decides the test, a crawl ordered by the walk that couples allowance and transfer edges reached the contracts with the most user-account demand sooner than a breadth-first crawl but not sooner than a crawl ordered by the number of contract backlinks, which was sooner. In the same run the transfer walk AWP did reach them sooner than the count it smooths, and the walks on allowance edges alone did not on inflow; where a visit reveals out-edges only the coupled walk led both comparators, without a verdict. Every crawl stayed far from the ideal order. Out of window, PageRank on the latest allowances ranked later new approval pairs below the count of approving contracts in both windows, and for most spenders it is a reweighted count, as its closed form shows; AWP ranked later new senders slightly above the transfer in-degree overall and, in the first window, below it among spenders that a contract had already paid. The next steps are a discovery-order test on a later freeze, fixed before its data exist, importance labels from outside the chain, and a better detection of smart accounts.
